The Main Types of Power Semiconductor Switches

  • Diodes
  • MOSFETs
  • IGBTs
  • Thyristors
  • Bidirectional switches
  • Etc.

For now, for each one, three questions:

  • Can we control when it turns on, and when it turns off?
  • Which current direction can it conduct when on?
  • Which voltage polarity can it block when off?

Picking a device for a real application brings in much more: ratings, losses, switching speed, cost. Here we only introduce the devices and their basic terminal characteristics.

Reading an Operating-Region Plot

  • References are fixed: \(i_{sw}\) flows into the \(+\) terminal of \(v_{sw}\)
  • Off: \(i_{sw}=0\), the switch sits on the \(v_{sw}\) axis and blocks \(v_{sw}\)
  • On: \(v_{sw}\approx 0\), the switch sits on the \(i_{sw}\) axis and conducts \(i_{sw}\)
  • A shaded quadrant means the switch can block voltage of that polarity and conduct current in that direction

Diodes

  • Uncontrollable: whether a diode is on or off depends on the circuit it is connected to
  • Conducts \(i_{sw}>0\), blocks \(v_{sw}<0\): quadrant II

MOSFETs

  • Controllable: turns on and off from the gate
  • Conducts current of either polarity
  • Blocks positive voltage only

IGBTs

  • Controllable
  • Conducts current in the positive direction only
  • Blocks positive voltage only

IGBT with Anti-Parallel Diode

  • Controllable (the IGBT part)
  • Conducts current in both directions: positive through the IGBT, negative through the diode
  • Blocks positive voltage only

Examples of Commercial IGBT Modules

Source: dynexsemi.com

Thyristors

  • Turn-on is controllable: a gate pulse while \(v_{sw}>0\)
  • Turn-off is not controllable: the external circuit must take its current to zero
  • Blocks both polarities, conducts positive current

Examples of Commercial Thyristors

Source: dynexsemi.com

Bidirectional Switches

  • Controllable in both directions: one gate per direction
  • Blocks both polarities, conducts both directions: all four quadrants
  • One gate on, the other off: behaves as a diode
  • One device in place of two back-to-back switches

Power Devices: Operating Regions

Same references, device rotated by 180°: every shaded quadrant moves to the opposite one, \((v,i)\to(-v,-i)\). The plot tells us the device and which way round to connect it.

Alternate Perspective: Rotate the Device by 180°

Same references, device rotated by 180°: every shaded quadrant moves to the opposite one, \((v,i)\to(-v,-i)\). The plot tells us the device and which way round to connect it.

Q: How do we know which switch type to use?

Choosing a Switch Type

  • Label \(v_{sw}\) and \(i_{sw}\) on each switch as on the device plots: \(+\) and \(i_{sw}\) both at the top terminal
  • Switch on: the sign of \(i_{sw}\) it must conduct
  • Switch off: the sign of \(v_{sw}\) it must block
  • Together they fix the quadrant(s) it must operate in
  • Pick a device whose shaded quadrants cover them all, as drawn or rotated by 180°: the plot says which terminal goes at the top

Example: Two Switches Between Vg and Vo

  • A battery \(V_o\) at the output: \(P = V_o I_L\) can flow either way
  • Small ripple: \(i_L \approx I_L\), so \(i_L\) keeps the sign of \(I_L\)
  • Three cases:
    1. \(I_L > 0\): \(P\) from \(V_g\) to \(V_o\)
    2. \(I_L < 0\): \(P\) from \(V_o\) to \(V_g\)
    3. \(I_L\) either sign, set by the operating point: \(P\) both ways

The Two Switch States

\(S_1\) on: \(\;i_1 = i_L\)

\(S_2\) off: blocks \(v_2 = +V_g\)

\(S_2\) on: \(\;i_2 = -i_L\)

\(S_1\) off: blocks \(v_1 = +V_g\)

Every case: both switches block \(+V_g\); only the current signs change, with \(i_L\)

Case 1: Power from Vg to Vo

\(S_1\): on \(\;i_1 = i_L > 0\), off \(\;v_1 = +V_g\)

\(S_2\): on \(\;i_2 = -i_L < 0\), off \(\;v_2 = +V_g\)

  • \(S_1\), quadrant I: a MOSFET or IGBT, drain (collector) toward \(V_g\)
  • \(S_2\), quadrant IV: a diode, cathode at the switch node
  • The buck converter of Lecture 2

Case 2: Power from Vo to Vg

\(S_1\): on \(\;i_1 = i_L < 0\), off \(\;v_1 = +V_g\)

\(S_2\): on \(\;i_2 = -i_L > 0\), off \(\;v_2 = +V_g\)

  • \(S_1\), quadrant IV: a diode turned over, cathode toward \(V_g\)
  • \(S_2\), quadrant I: a MOSFET or IGBT, drain at the switch node
  • Right to left: a boost from \(V_o\) to \(V_g\)

Case 3: Power Either Way

\(S_1\): on \(\;i_1 = i_L\), either sign, off \(\;v_1 = +V_g\)

\(S_2\): on \(\;i_2 = -i_L\), either sign, off \(\;v_2 = +V_g\)

  • Both need quadrants I and IV: a MOSFET, or an IGBT with an anti-parallel diode
  • One circuit: a buck from \(V_g\) to \(V_o\) and a boost back
